title: Social Video Sizes for TikTok, Reels | AIVideosUGC
description: Match the file to TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, or Shorts. Make a tall 9:16, a square 1:1, or a wide 16:9 from a product photo, then download and post.
h1: Social Video Sizes for TikTok and Reels
lead: Stop guessing social media video sizes. You match the file to the app and keep your product large. Each shape is its own file, and you see the credit cost before it runs.
secondary_keywords: square ads for the Facebook feed
summary: Make the tall 9:16 file first, then add a square feed and a wide 16:9 when you need it.

sections.h2: Eight Social Ad Formats That Stop a Scroll
paras: You can open on a beat, a short how-to, or a joke. Pick the format, then pick the shape, and keep your product large.
Catch the moment fast. You time one product move to a track buyers still hear, and the tall file keeps that move large.
Teach one useful step. You turn a short script into a how-to, with an AI actor or your product alone, and the words stay readable.
Show a real day with your product. You upload clips from a normal day, trim the long pauses, add captions, and keep your product in the middle.
Reply to one real comment. You answer on screen, keep your product large, and export that reply as a tall file or a square.
Name the three things a buyer checks. You use quick cuts and words on screen, and your product stays in frame.
Show how you pack an order. You join short clips of packing and the first use into one story, with your product kept large.
Set a calm mood. You pair a soft shot, a short line, and a gentle track, often as a square on your profile.
Land the joke, then the product. You cut to your product while the laugh is still clear, and you keep the label easy to read.

sections.h2: A Native Size for Each App
paras: Each app needs a file that already fills its screen. You make a separate file for TikTok, for Instagram, for YouTube, and for Facebook, so your product stays large.

Shorts need their own tall file, so the phone is full and your product stays large. A wide YouTube screen takes a separate 16:9 file for a longer demo. You do not drop the wide file into the tall Shorts slot. See [YouTube Shorts](page:plat-youtube-shorts).

Instagram Reels want the tall file, and Stories want that same tall file. The scrolling feed can take a square, and a square in the tall slot leaves bars. You make the feed file and the tall file as two jobs.
A 9:16 file fills the TikTok screen, so your product stays large. A wide clip on an upright phone shrinks to a strip. You build the tall file with [AI UGC video ads](page:video-ads).
A LinkedIn post can be square or wide, so people can pause and read. You keep the words large. You match the spoken line to the product page.
Facebook can use a square in the feed and a tall file for the full-screen spot. You build that file on its own so your product stays large. You check the crop before you pay to run it.

sections.h2: Native 1080 Specs for Reels and Shorts
paras: Do not let a bad crop hide your product. You match the shape to the feed, from a wide 16:9 to a tall 9:16, and these are shapes, not one fixed pixel size.
16:9 is the wide shape. It fills a laptop, a longer demo, or a desktop feed. You use it for a tutorial or a product demo. A full phone screen wants the tall file instead.

9:16 is the tall shape, and it fills a phone. Names sit at the top, and like and share sit on the right. You keep your product and any words in the middle, clear of those buttons. A 1080x1920 file is a common export of this tall shape.
1:1 is the square shape. It fills a Facebook or Instagram feed and a row of cards. A still photo can use this shape too. A 1080x1080 file is a common export of this square.

4:3 is a little wider than a square, and 3:4 is a little taller. You use them when a placement lists that shape. For other jobs, pick 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9 on the setup screen. For current Shorts file rules, see [YouTube Shorts size rules](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/16041697?hl=en-GB).

sections.h2: Why Make a Native Size for Every App
paras: Skip a long night of cutting. One product photo can feed a tall file and a square file, and each job shows its credit cost before you start.
Open on a detail other ads skip. You pick a track buyers still hear this week.
Want a different first second? You choose the pause before your product appears. Put that pause in your own script.
Tired of filming every size? You can post with an AI actor from the [actor library](page:ai-actors), or show only your product. Anyone on screen is an AI actor you chose for the shop.
Already have a product page? A fact on that page can become the spoken line in a tall file, next to the photo you took. See [URL to video](page:url-to-video).

sections.h2: How Four Shops Split the Sizes
paras: You get a 9:16 file and a 1:1 file from the same product photo. You skip an evening of cutting one video apart, and you post the size that fills the placement.
You run a one-product shop, so you get a second opening without a new photo. You keep the photo and the offer, change the first line, and run both files.
You sell alone, so you leave the frame on the product and add a spoken line. You post the tall file where the phone screen is full.
You sell in two languages, so you keep the same product and replace the spoken line. The shape stays the one that fills that placement.

sections.h2: Ad Styles for What You Sell
paras: From a fast joke to a calm routine. You match the pace to your product, and you keep the label easy to see.
Land the joke, then the label. If the joke comes first, you cut to the label before the laugh ends, and you keep your product readable.
Show your product in a routine. A routine or a texture shot shows your product in context. You hold the real item next to the screen and check the shade before you post.
Keep one motion readable. One motion is enough. You keep the words in the middle, where the buttons leave them readable on a phone.
Show it closed, then open. The color stays the same in both frames. You show the back only when your photo includes the back.
Answer one how-to on camera. A teaching clip can show how to use it, while your product stays easy to see.
Leave the frame on the product. Faceless posts run with you off camera. You leave the frame on the product, add captions, and let a voice read the offer. Match that offer to the product page.

sections.h2: What the Editor Handles for You
paras: The chores that took three apps now sit in one pass. You still choose the line and the shape.
You get a first second that fits your product. The track can match a slow shot. You still pick the line.
A brand that never shows a face can still have a spoken line. You leave the frame on the product, and you put that line in the captions.
Cuts can land on a beat. Cuts can land on a beat you pick from the music library. A product move can sit on that same beat.
You get a script you can edit. It is written from the product page, like a reply to a shopper. You change the line before the job starts.

A photo or a link can start it. A photo you already took is enough to start the clip. [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) is the way in. A product link is the other door when the page already lists the size and the texture.
Finish in one place. Captions, the spoken voice, and the song live in the editor. You can change how the words look, and you can make several openings from the same photo.

sections.h2: From One Photo to the Right File in Minutes
paras: You spend your time on the shape and the line. The trim between frames is already handled for you.
A photo of the whole product is the usual start. A product link works when the page already shows that item. You bring your own clip when you want the pace of something you filmed.
You mark the second where the label has to be readable. The rest of the timing can flex around that one second.
You pick one shape for this job: 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4. A second shape is a separate job.
The spoken line sits in the middle, clear of the bottom and the right edge, where the app covers words. A song can wait until this pass looks right.
You download the file. Nothing is printed over your product. Play the file on your phone before you pay to run the ad, and check that your product is still centered.
A video is 24 credits for 6 seconds, 40 for 10, 60 for 15, or 120 for 30. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits. Pro is $35 for 300 credits, and Premium is $63 for 600.

faq.q: Can I edit a video to match the music?
faq.a: Yes. Match product movement and scene changes to the music. Keep the product and message easy to see even in a fast edit.

faq.q: Can I turn a wide video into a vertical ad?
faq.a: Yes. Make a vertical 9:16 version and check that the product and captions fit the phone screen. You can use the same idea in another size without filming again.

faq.q: Are the music and the spoken voice safe to use in an ad?
faq.a: Yes, use music and voices supplied for commercial use. Clear any audio you upload yourself, and check the ad platform’s current rules before posting.

faq.q: Can I change how the words on screen look?
faq.a: Yes. Choose captions that fit your brand’s colors and are easy to read on a phone. You can adjust them before exporting.

faq.q: Can I start from a product page or a short article?
faq.a: Yes. Paste a product page or short article to start the message, or upload your own photo. Review the words and visuals before generating.

faq.q: Can the same ad run in another language?
faq.a: Yes. Make another version with a translated message and matching voice. You can reach another audience without filming a new ad.

faq.q: Which shape should a small shop make first?
faq.a: Start with 9:16 for Stories, Reels, and Shorts. Add 1:1 for square feeds or 16:9 for wide placements when you need them.

faq.q: Can I post without showing my face?
faq.a: Yes. Show the product with a voiceover, or choose an AI actor to present it. You can make a short ad without appearing on camera.
